title: Implementation of OR Gate from NAND Gate
excerpt: NAND is functionally complete, so a OR gate can be built from it alone. Here is the construction, and why it works.
seoTitle: OR Gate Using NAND Gates: Circuit and Truth Table
seoDescription: How to implement a OR gate using only NAND gates, with the step-by-step construction, boolean expression and full truth table.

content.text: The NAND gate is functionally complete, which means every other gate can be built from it alone, and this page builds an OR gate from nothing else. Along the way you will see why the construction works and how many gates it costs.

body.text: Why OR can be built from NAND

content.text: This one is De Morgan's law made physical: A OR B is the same as NOT((NOT A) AND (NOT B)). Invert both inputs, NAND them, and OR falls out.
Functional completeness is the reason chip designers care: a fab only has to get one gate right, and every circuit can be built from copies of it.
NAND and NOR are both functionally complete
; no other two-input gate is, on its own.

Build the circuit, then check every row. If all four match, the construction is correct: a truth table is a complete specification for a combinational circuit, so agreeing on every row means the two circuits are the same function.

. Gate count matters in real hardware because every gate costs area, power and a small propagation delay, which is why a circuit built entirely from one gate type is usually larger than the same logic built from mixed gates.

Reading the construction is not the same as getting it working. Open the editor, drop in the gates, and watch the output change as you toggle the inputs, since that is the only way to be sure the circuit does what the truth table claims.

Every conversion in this track follows the same two moves: get the un-inverted version, then cancel or add an inversion. Once you have seen OR built this way, the rest are variations on the same idea. The wider digital logic track covers where these gates end up, in adders, latches, and memory.
